items.prompt: What is a "rollback" in the sense this unit uses it?
choices: Reverting a system to its previous known-good deployed state after a bad deploy
A code review process that a team runs on every pull request before any deploy
A type of automated test suite that only ever runs right after a deploy finishes
The act of renaming a git branch back to whatever its original name used to be
items.explanation: A rollback specifically means reverting to the previous deployed state, as distinct from testing, review, or unrelated git operations.
items.reference:
↩️ rollback = revert to the previous known-good deployed state
➕ fix-forward = ship a new correction on top of the bad version

Why: These are two different responses to a bad deploy — confusing them means reaching for the wrong tool during an incident.

items.prompt: How does a rollback differ from a "fix forward" deploy?
choices: A rollback reverts to a previous state; a fix-forward deploy ships a new correction on top of the bad version instead of reverting
They are simply two different names engineers use for the exact same underlying action
A rollback always requires a full database restore, while fix-forward is said to never require one
Fix-forward is described as only applying to frontend deploys, rollback only to backend ones
items.explanation: L1 defines rollback specifically as reverting, in contrast to fixing forward with a new deploy — they're two distinct incident responses, not the same thing under different names.
items.reference:
↩️ rollback = revert to the previous known-good deployed state
➕ fix-forward = ship a new correction on top of the bad version

Why: These are two different responses to a bad deploy — confusing them means reaching for the wrong tool during an incident.

items.prompt: In L1's Scenario, was the 40-minute rollback slow because the on-call engineer took a long time to decide to roll back?
choices: No — the decision was fast; the mechanics of actually performing the rollback (rebuilding from source) were the bottleneck
Yes — the Scenario states the engineer spent most of the 40 minutes debating whether to roll back at all
Yes, because the Scenario says the engineer tried three other unrelated fixes before finally rolling back
It's genuinely not stated in the Scenario whether the decision or the mechanics took longer
items.explanation: L1 is explicit: the decision to roll back was fast, and the 40 minutes was lost in rebuilding the artifact from source — a preparation problem, not a decision problem.
items.reference:
🔥 deciding to roll back: fast
🐢 rebuilding from source: 40 minutes

Why: Rollback speed is mostly a preparation problem — whether a ready artifact already exists — not a decision-making problem.

items.prompt: What made the difference between the 40-minute team and the 2-minute team in L1's facts?
choices: Whether a previous deployable artifact was already ready to redeploy, decided before the incident started
The 2-minute team simply had a larger on-call team actively staffed that particular night
The 40-minute team's underlying bug happened to be objectively more severe than the other's
The 2-minute team is described as having skipped verifying the rollback actually fixed anything
items.explanation: The gap is entirely about preparation made in advance — having a ready artifact — not team size, bug severity, or skipped verification.
items.reference:
🔥 deciding to roll back: fast
🐢 rebuilding from source: 40 minutes

Why: Rollback speed is mostly a preparation problem — whether a ready artifact already exists — not a decision-making problem.

items.prompt: What is a "deployable artifact"?
choices: The built, ready-to-run output of a deploy (like a container image or compiled binary), as opposed to the source code it was built from
The written documentation that explains, in prose, how a particular deploy process is supposed to work
A snapshot backup of the production database taken as a precaution right before a deploy runs
The ticket or formal approval record that's attached to a deploy before it's allowed to ship
items.explanation: A deployable artifact is the built, runnable output — not documentation, a database backup, or an approval record.
items.reference:
💾 deployable artifact = the built, ready-to-run output (image/binary)
📄 source code = what it was built from, not the same thing

Why: Rollback speed depends on whether the artifact still exists, not whether the source still exists — source has to be rebuilt.

items.prompt: Why does having source code in version control not guarantee a fast rollback?
choices: Because turning source code into a running artifact requires a build step, which takes time if it has to happen again during an incident
Because version control systems are described as not reliably storing old commits once newer ones exist
Because source code technically cannot be checked out again once a newer commit has been merged
Because performing a rollback directly from source code is described as forbidden by convention
items.explanation: The gap between source and a running artifact is the build step — that's exactly the tax the Scenario's team paid when they had to rebuild during the incident.
items.reference:
💾 deployable artifact = the built, ready-to-run output (image/binary)
📄 source code = what it was built from, not the same thing

Why: Rollback speed depends on whether the artifact still exists, not whether the source still exists — source has to be rebuilt.

items.prompt: What is a "backward-compatible migration"?
choices: A schema change written so that both the old and new application code can run correctly against it
A migration that is restricted to only ever adding new indexes, never adding new columns
A migration that has specifically been reviewed and signed off by at least two engineers
A migration that happens to be undoable with a single, short SQL command
items.explanation: Backward-compatibility is about both code versions working against the same schema at once — not about indexes specifically, review process, or undo mechanics.
items.reference:
✅ backward-compatible = old code AND new code both work against the schema
⚠️ without it, a code rollback can crash against the new schema

Why: A rollback that reverts code but not the schema can leave the system worse off than the original bug.

items.prompt: Why can a rollback that reverts application code still leave a system broken?
choices: If the bad deploy also changed the database schema in a way the old code can't handle, the old code may crash against the new schema
Because git is described as not actually supporting reverting a repository to an older commit
Because performing a rollback always requires restarting every single server across the fleet
Because code that's reverted is said to automatically lose access to its production secrets
items.explanation: The database migration trap is exactly this: code and schema must agree, and a rollback that only reverts code can leave them mismatched.
items.reference:
✅ backward-compatible = old code AND new code both work against the schema
⚠️ without it, a code rollback can crash against the new schema

Why: A rollback that reverts code but not the schema can leave the system worse off than the original bug.

items.prompt: What is a "health check" in the context of rollback strategy?
choices: An automated signal, like error rate or latency, watched continuously after a deploy to judge whether it's behaving correctly
A manual checklist that an engineer fills out exactly once, before a deploy is allowed to start
A test suite that is described as only ever being run inside a staging environment
A short survey sent out to users afterward, asking whether the app subjectively feels slow
items.explanation: A health check is specifically an automated, continuous signal — not a pre-deploy checklist, a staging-only test suite, or a user survey.

items.prompt: Why does a health check need to be continuous rather than a one-time check right after a deploy finishes?
choices: Because some regressions only show up after real traffic accumulates, not in the instant a deploy completes
Because continuous health checks are described as required by law in most jurisdictions
Because running a one-time check instead is said to use too much CPU to be practical
Continuous checking is not actually necessary, since a one-time check is described as equally effective
items.explanation: L1/L2 frame health checks as watching over time specifically because problems can take real traffic to surface — a snapshot at deploy time would miss that.

items.prompt: What does "rollback trigger" refer to?
choices: The condition that starts a rollback — either automatic (a health check crosses a threshold) or manual (a human reviews and decides)
The specific git command an engineer types in order to revert a single problematic commit
A physical button that's described as present in a deployment dashboard's user interface
The name of whichever engineer happens to be on-call during a given incident
items.explanation: A rollback trigger is the condition that starts the rollback — automatic or manual — not a specific command, UI element, or person's name.

items.prompt: Per L1, can a rollback trigger be either automatic or manual?
choices: Yes — a health check crossing a threshold can trigger it automatically, or a person can review an ambiguous signal and decide manually
No — per L1, rollback triggers are described as always having to be fully manual, with no exceptions
No — per L1, rollback triggers are described as always having to be fully automatic, with no exceptions
L1 states rollback triggers are decided by a formal vote taken among the entire engineering team
items.explanation: L1 explicitly defines the trigger as either automatic or manual, depending on the situation — not exclusively one or the other.

items.prompt: Per L1, when should a rollback strategy be designed, relative to when an incident happens?
choices: Before the incident — designed in advance, not improvised live during an incident
During the incident itself, only once the exact underlying bug is fully understood by the team
Only after the incident has fully resolved, as one part of the written post-mortem
Rollback strategy is described as not actually needing any advance design work at all
items.explanation: L1 draws the same connection incident-response makes: a plan decided in advance is more reliable than one improvised under pressure, live.

items.prompt: Given the migration trap L2 describes, does that mean risky deploys should just avoid database migrations entirely?
choices: No — migrations need to be written so both code versions can run against the same schema at once for as long as a rollback might happen (expand-contract), not avoided entirely
Yes — L2 concludes migrations should never run alongside any deploy that also changes application code at all
Yes, but this conclusion is described as only applying to deploys made outside normal business hours
No, but L2 is described as concluding rollback itself should be abandoned whenever migrations are involved
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that the fix is writing rollback-compatible migrations (like expand-contract), not avoiding migrations altogether — avoidance isn't the lesson, compatibility is.

items.prompt: Per L2, what closes the gap between "source code still exists" and "a rollback happens instantly"?
choices: Keeping the previous deploy's build artifact around after it's superseded, so a rollback redeploys it instead of rebuilding it
Writing noticeably more detailed commit messages so engineers can locate the right commit faster
Requiring two separate human approvals before any deploy is allowed to go out at all
Simply increasing the total number of engineers staffed on the on-call rotation each week
items.explanation: L2's core fast-rollback mechanic is retention of the previous build artifact — not commit messages, approvals, or staffing.
items.reference:
📦 keep the previous artifact ready — don't discard it after a successful deploy
♻️ rollback = redeploy that existing artifact, same mechanism as a forward deploy

Why: Deleting old artifacts to save storage turns every future rollback into a rebuild-from-source under incident pressure.

items.prompt: A team deletes container images for any version older than the currently-running one, right after each successful deploy. What will their next rollback look like?
choices: Slow — there's no ready artifact for the previous version, so a rollback has to rebuild it from source first
Fast — deleting the old images is described as having no effect whatsoever on rollback speed
Fast, but only if the rollback happens to occur within the first hour of the new deploy going out
It's described as depending only on how many replicas the service currently happens to be running
items.explanation: This is exactly the failure mode L2's Checkpoint covers — discarding the previous artifact removes the thing that makes rollback fast, forcing a rebuild under pressure.
items.reference:
📦 keep the previous artifact ready — don't discard it after a successful deploy
♻️ rollback = redeploy that existing artifact, same mechanism as a forward deploy

Why: Deleting old artifacts to save storage turns every future rollback into a rebuild-from-source under incident pressure.

items.prompt: Per L2's migration pattern table, is dropping a column the old code still reads rollback-compatible?
choices: No — the old code will crash or error trying to read a column that no longer exists
Yes — dropping a column is described as always safe as long as the drop itself happens quickly
Yes, as long as the dropped column was entirely empty (all null values) before it was removed
It's described as depending only on which specific database engine the team happens to be using
items.explanation: L2's table is explicit: dropping a column the old code reads breaks that old code the moment it's redeployed — not safe regardless of speed, emptiness, or engine.
items.reference:
❌ Drop a column old code readsold code crashes
❌ Rename in placeone version always mismatches
✅ Add nullable columnold code ignores it
✅ Expand-contractboth versions work until the later drop

Why: Rollback safety depends on whether the OLD code, not just the new code, can still run against the current schema.

items.prompt: Per L2's migration pattern table, is renaming a column in place, in the same deploy as a code change, rollback-compatible?
choices: No — whichever code version doesn't match the current name (old or new) breaks
Yes — renaming a column is described as always safe, since the underlying data itself is unchanged
Yes, as long as the rename happens to run inside a separate database transaction
It's described as only unsafe for renamed primary-key columns, safe for every other kind
items.explanation: A straight rename means only one code version's expected column name is correct at any moment — exactly like a drop, just with a different failure mode.
items.reference:
❌ Drop a column old code readsold code crashes
❌ Rename in placeone version always mismatches
✅ Add nullable columnold code ignores it
✅ Expand-contractboth versions work until the later drop

Why: Rollback safety depends on whether the OLD code, not just the new code, can still run against the current schema.

items.prompt: What is the "expand-contract" pattern?
choices: Add the new column first and write both old and new, then drop the old column only in a later, separate deploy after the rollback window has passed
Expand the database's total storage capacity first, then contract it back down after a migration finishes
Run the same migration twice — once expanded across every shard, then contracted back to just one
A general technique for compressing database backups more tightly before archiving them long-term
items.explanation: Expand-contract specifically means splitting a schema change into an additive step and a much-later removal step — not about storage capacity, sharding, or backups.
items.reference:
1️⃣ expand: add the new column, write both, remove nothing
2️⃣ contract: drop the old column, only in a LATER separate deploy

Why: Splitting the risky code deploy from the schema cleanup means the deploy that might get rolled back never depends on something being removed.

items.prompt: Why does expand-contract put the column drop in a separate, later deploy instead of the same deploy as the code change?
choices: So the risky code deploy, which might need a rollback, never depends on something already removed — the drop happens once rollback is no longer a realistic concern
Because most databases are described as technically forbidding more than one schema change per single deploy
Because the code change and the schema drop are required to always be reviewed by two separate engineers
Simply to reduce the total number of git commits that end up attached to that particular feature
items.explanation: The whole point of separating the steps is timing: the drop is safe only once the code deploy's rollback window has passed, so it's deliberately pushed to its own later deploy.
items.reference:
1️⃣ expand: add the new column, write both, remove nothing
2️⃣ contract: drop the old column, only in a LATER separate deploy

Why: Splitting the risky code deploy from the schema cleanup means the deploy that might get rolled back never depends on something being removed.

items.prompt: Per L2, when is it appropriate to let a rollback happen fully automatically, without a human decision?
choices: When the failure signature is sharp, sustained, and well-understood — unambiguous enough that a machine acting alone is low-risk
Only during normal business hours, and never automatically overnight, according to L2
Only for deploys that change fewer than some specific threshold number of files
Never — L2 is described as stating that every single rollback must always involve a human decision
items.explanation: L2's flowchart routes unambiguous, clearly-over-threshold signals to automatic rollback, and ambiguous ones to a human — the deciding factor is signal certainty, not time of day or deploy size.

items.prompt: Per L2, why isn't a slow, mild uptick in latency automatically rolled back the same way a sharp error-rate spike is?
choices: Because a mild, ambiguous signal might just be an unrelated traffic pattern, and automating a rollback on it risks reverting a perfectly good deploy over noise
Because latency metrics are described as technically impossible to monitor in an automated way
Because only error rate, and never latency, is described in L2 as a valid health signal at all
Because mild signals are described as always turning out to be false alarms, so they get ignored entirely
items.explanation: L2 draws the line at ambiguity, not at which metric is involved — an ambiguous latency uptick is exactly the kind of signal better left to a human's broader context.

items.prompt: A deploy ships a code change and, in the same deploy, a migration that drops a column the old code reads. If the new code turns out to be buggy, what's the actual risk of redeploying the old code as a rollback?
choices: The old code will error or crash reading a column that the migration already removed, potentially making things worse than the original bug
There's no real risk at all — redeploying old code is described as always safe regardless of schema changes
The only risk described is a brief increase in overall deploy time, not any actual functional break
The risk is described as only applying in the specific case where the dropped column was the primary key
items.explanation: This is L2's central nuance: a code-only rollback assumes the schema underneath hasn't moved in an incompatible way — when it has, the 'safe' rollback isn't actually safe.

items.prompt: How does L2 connect blue-green deployment and feature flags (from progressive-delivery) to this unit's rollback model?
choices: Both are concrete instances of keeping the known-good state ready — a warm second environment, or a flag that flips a behavior off instantly without a redeploy
They are described as entirely unrelated to rollback strategy, relevant only to gradual traffic exposure
Blue-green and feature flags are both described as slower than a standard artifact-based rollback in every case
L2 states that only feature flags, never blue-green deployment, count as a genuine rollback mechanism here
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames both as the same underlying principle as a ready build artifact — having the known-good state prepared in advance — just implemented at different layers.

items.prompt: Per L2 (and L1's incident-response connection), why is deciding "what does rollback mean for this system" a bad thing to figure out live, during an incident?
choices: Because that is exactly the moment the decision is most likely to be made badly — the same reasoning incident-response applies to disclosure and post-mortems being pre-planned
Because most incident-response tooling is described as technically locking every configuration change mid-incident
Because engineers are described as contractually required to document a rollback plan before any deploy
It is not actually described as a problem — L2 states live decisions mid-incident are usually higher quality
items.explanation: L1/L2 draw a direct parallel to incident-response's pre-planning principle: decisions made under live incident pressure are worse than the same decisions made calmly in advance.

items.prompt: Per L2's overall model, does a rollback strategy consist of a single decision, or several separate concerns?
choices: Several separate concerns: how fast reverting can happen, whether reverting is actually safe given the schema, and what triggers the revert
A single decision: whichever engineer happens to be on-call simply chooses to revert that night or not
A single technical setting: specifically how many replicas the deployment happens to currently be running
L2 states rollback strategy reduces entirely to picking the right confirmation-window size alone
items.explanation: L2 explicitly separates speed (artifact readiness), safety (migration compatibility), and triggering (automatic vs. manual) as three distinct concerns that together make up a rollback strategy, not one single decision.

items.prompt: Complete decideRollbackAction(state, metrics, config) so it returns { action: 'rollback' } once errorRate (errors/sampleSize) reaches or exceeds config.severeErrorRateThreshold, without needing any consecutive bad windows first. Assume sampleSize always meets config.minSampleSize in these tests.

tests.description: a severe error rate triggers immediate rollback
an error rate below the severe threshold does not roll back

items.explanation: A severe error rate is unambiguous enough that the function shouldn't wait for consecutive confirmation windows — it should bypass the counters entirely and act immediately, exactly like L3's classifyWindow/decideRollbackAction pair does for its 'severe' classification.
items.reference:
🚨 severe = errorRate above the severe threshold
⚡ severe skips the confirmation counters entirely

Why: Waiting for confirmation on an unambiguous spike only costs time without buying real confidence.

items.prompt: This buggy decideRollbackAction checks errorRate against config.severeErrorRateThreshold using the wrong comparison (> instead of >=), so a window exactly at the threshold is missed. Fix the comparison.

tests.description: an error rate exactly at the severe threshold triggers rollback
an error rate above the severe threshold still triggers rollback

items.explanation: config.severeErrorRateThreshold is meant to be the boundary that counts as severe, so a window exactly at that rate should still trigger a rollback — that requires >=, not a strict >, which would silently let a threshold-exact spike through as merely 'watching'.
items.reference:
🚨 severe = errorRate above the severe threshold
⚡ severe skips the confirmation counters entirely

Why: Waiting for confirmation on an unambiguous spike only costs time without buying real confidence.

items.prompt: Complete countConsecutiveBad(windows, isBad) so it returns the length of the longest run of consecutive 'bad' windows at the END of the array (a trailing streak), given isBad(window) returns true/false per window. If the array ends on a good window, the answer is 0.

tests.description: three bad windows in a row at the end returns 3
ending on a good window returns 0
all windows bad returns the full length

items.explanation: The decision function only cares about the current trailing streak, not the whole history, so this walks backward from the end and stops at the first good window — mirroring how decideRollbackAction's consecutiveBadWindows counter resets to 0 the instant a good window appears.

items.prompt: This buggy countConsecutiveBad counts bad windows across the WHOLE array instead of just the trailing streak at the end, so an old bad window earlier in the array wrongly still gets counted even after a good window has since occurred. Fix it so only the trailing run counts.

tests.description: a bad window followed by a good window at the end returns 0, not 1

items.explanation: Summing bad windows across the entire history ignores that a good window should reset the streak — the fix walks backward from the end and stops at the first good window, so only the current unbroken trailing run counts, matching the state machine's own reset-on-good behavior.

items.prompt: What does "flapping" mean in the context of an automatic rollback trigger?
choices: A trigger so sensitive that ordinary metric noise repeatedly rolls back perfectly healthy deploys
A deploy that deliberately alternates between two different versions on purpose, for A/B testing
A health check that never returns any result at all and simply hangs indefinitely
A rollback that technically succeeds but ends up taking longer than the original deploy did
items.explanation: Flapping is specifically about over-sensitivity causing repeated unnecessary rollbacks on noise — not intentional A/B alternation, a hang, or a slow-but-successful rollback.
items.reference:
🪢 too sensitive → flapping: healthy deploys get rolled back on noise
🐌 too conservative → slow: a real regression runs for a long time before anything acts

Why: The confirmation-window size is a real trade-off with no single correct value — it depends on the system's own baseline noise.

items.prompt: L3's Scenario B (a single noisy blip, then three good windows) resulted in 'healthy', not 'rollback'. What would have changed that outcome if badWindowsToTriggerRollback had been set to 1 instead of 3?
choices: The single blip alone would have triggered an unnecessary rollback of a perfectly healthy deploy — this is exactly what flapping looks like
Nothing would change at all — the described outcome does not depend on that configuration value
It would have simply taken longer to reach 'healthy', but still never have triggered a rollback
The severe threshold would have activated instead, rolling back immediately regardless of that setting
items.explanation: L3 states this directly: with the confirmation requirement lowered to 1, the same noisy blip that Scenario B correctly absorbed would have caused a false-positive rollback instead.
items.reference:
🪢 too sensitive → flapping: healthy deploys get rolled back on noise
🐌 too conservative → slow: a real regression runs for a long time before anything acts

Why: The confirmation-window size is a real trade-off with no single correct value — it depends on the system's own baseline noise.

items.prompt: Per L3, what's the cost of setting badWindowsToTriggerRollback very high (e.g. 10) to avoid flapping entirely?
choices: A real regression now runs in production for many more windows before anything acts, undercutting the speed benefit automation was meant to provide
There is no downside described at all — a higher number is treated as strictly better in every situation
It's described as only affecting how the rollback gets logged, not when it actually happens
It's described as causing the severe-threshold bypass to stop working entirely
items.explanation: L3 is explicit: over-conservative tuning reintroduces the exact slowness problem this whole unit opened with, just with extra steps.

items.prompt: Per L3, is there a single universally correct value for badWindowsToTriggerRollback that every system should use?
choices: No — the right value depends on how noisy a system's baseline metrics are and how costly a false-positive rollback is versus extra minutes of a real regression
Yes — L3 states 3 consecutive windows is described as the universal industry standard across every system
Yes — the correct value is described as always being exactly equal to the number of replicas running
No such value can ever be chosen; L3 is described as arguing triggers should never use consecutive windows at all
items.explanation: L3 explicitly rejects a one-size-fits-all number — it's a tuning trade-off specific to each system's own traffic and cost profile.

items.prompt: In L3's unsafe migration example, what specifically breaks if v42 is bad and the team redeploys v41 after legacy_status has already been dropped?
choices: Every call to getOrderSummary in v41 throws, because it reads a column (legacy_status) that no longer exists in the schema
Nothing breaks at all — the rollback is described as succeeding and the incident fully resolving
Only new orders created after the rollback are described as being affected, not existing ones
The rollback is described as silently succeeding, but order statuses display as blank for all users
items.explanation: L3 traces the exact failure: v41's getOrderSummary function reads legacy_status directly, and that column is gone, so every call throws — a new, guaranteed incident on top of the original bug.
items.reference:
❌ unsafe: drop legacy_status in the same deploy → v41 rollback crashes reading it
✅ safe: add order_status, write both, drop legacy_status only in a LATER deploy

Why: A rollback is only as safe as the least backward-compatible thing shipped alongside it.

items.prompt: In L3's safe (expand-contract) rewrite, why is v41 unaffected even while v42 is live and writing to both columns?
choices: Because v41 was never changed to know about order_status — it only ever reads legacy_status, which the expand step never touches
Because v41 is described as automatically detecting and adapting to schema changes at runtime
Because the database is described as rejecting any write to order_status whenever v41 is also running
Because v41 and v42 are described in L3 as running against entirely separate databases
items.explanation: The safety comes from what's NOT touched during the expand step — legacy_status stays exactly as v41 expects it, so a rollback to v41 during this window changes nothing about what v41 depends on.
items.reference:
❌ unsafe: drop legacy_status in the same deploy → v41 rollback crashes reading it
✅ safe: add order_status, write both, drop legacy_status only in a LATER deploy

Why: A rollback is only as safe as the least backward-compatible thing shipped alongside it.

items.prompt: Per L3's closing section, does the migration-safety lesson only apply to databases, or does it generalize further?
choices: It generalizes to any coupled, independently-versioned pair, like a mobile app and its API, or a message queue producer and consumer
It applies strictly and only to relational database schemas, per L3's closing section
It's described as generalizing to literally any two files that live in the same codebase
L3 states the lesson does not generalize at all beyond this one exact worked example
items.explanation: L3 explicitly extends the core lesson (a rollback is only as safe as the least backward-compatible thing shipped with it) to any independently-versioned coupled pair, not just databases.

items.prompt: L3's extension question asks what happens if a bad deploy already accepted writes in a new, incompatible format before rollback triggered. What does this add to the migration-safety discussion?
choices: That redeploying old code alone may not be enough — data already written in the new format might also need its own repair step
Nothing new at all — L3 states this scenario is functionally identical to the ordinary expand-contract case
That this particular situation makes automatic rollback triggers entirely unnecessary going forward from here
That this situation is described as only able to occur if the severe-threshold bypass was never configured
items.explanation: This is exactly the extension L3 poses: a rollback undoes code and (with the right migration pattern) schema, but data already written under the bad format is a separate problem a code/schema rollback alone doesn't fix.

items.prompt: In classifyWindow, why does a window with too few requests (below minSampleSize) return 'insufficient-data' instead of being judged as good or bad?
choices: A rate computed from very few requests is unreliable — a small absolute number of errors can produce a misleadingly extreme rate at low volume
Because the function is described as designed to always favor 'good' when traffic is low, to avoid unnecessary rollbacks
Because computing any percentage at all is described as requiring at least 1,000 requests, by definition
It's described as an arbitrary safeguard with no real justification given anywhere in L3
items.explanation: L3's own Checkpoint covers this directly: 1 error out of 4 requests is a 25% rate that would look severe, but it's meaningless noise at that volume — insufficient-data avoids trusting a rate that small a sample can't support.
items.reference:
🔢 a rate from a tiny sample can swing wildly on a couple of errors
⏸️ insufficient-data = wait for more traffic before trusting the rate

Why: A computed rate only means something once there's enough volume behind it.

items.prompt: A deploy's health check window sees only 8 requests total, 2 of which errored (a 25% error rate, at or above a 25% severe threshold). Per classifyWindow's logic, should this trigger an immediate rollback?
choices: No — with minSampleSize unmet, classifyWindow should return 'insufficient-data' rather than trusting a rate computed from only 8 requests
Yes — any error rate at or above the severe threshold is described as triggering an immediate rollback regardless of sample size
Yes, but only because 2 raw errors is itself described as an unacceptably high absolute number
No, because classifyWindow is described as only ever evaluating latency, never error rate, at low traffic volumes
items.explanation: The sample-size check runs before the rate is even computed against thresholds — with too few requests, classifyWindow deliberately withholds judgment rather than acting on a rate that small a sample can't support.
items.reference:
🔢 a rate from a tiny sample can swing wildly on a couple of errors
⏸️ insufficient-data = wait for more traffic before trusting the rate

Why: A computed rate only means something once there's enough volume behind it.
